questions.explanation: The book walks through the web-orders topic: the fulfillment subscriber triggers fulfillment, and marketing runs real-time analytics or ML tuning.

questions.question: How does the book analogize stream partitions, and how are messages distributed among them?
options: Partitions are like the lanes of a multilane freeway, allowing parallelism and higher throughput; messages are distributed across partitions by partition key, and messages with the same partition key always end up in the same partition
Partitions are like pages in a book read in any order
Partitions distribute messages randomly with no key logic
Each partition can hold only one message
questions.explanation: The book says "a good analogy is a multilane freeway," with parallelism and higher throughput, and messages distributed by partition key, where the same key always lands in the same partition.

questions.question: How does the book illustrate a partition-key calculation, and what IoT pattern does it recommend?
options: Using a numeric message ID, you divide by 3 and take the remainder to pick among three partitions; in IoT, use a device ID as the partition key so all messages from a device go to the same processing server
Partitions are chosen by alphabetical order of the key
IoT devices must use the state as the partition key
Partition keys are assigned randomly at runtime
questions.explanation: The book's Figure 5-11 example divides a numeric ID by 3 and takes the remainder, and it recommends using a device ID as the partition key for IoT so each device's messages reach one processing server.

questions.question: Why are event-streaming platforms a good choice when you need reliable production, storage, and ingestion of event data?
options: They are typically distributed systems with streams stored on various nodes, so if a node goes down another replaces it and the stream is still accessible, meaning records aren't lost
They store all records on a single node
They delete records as soon as a node fails
They cannot replicate data across nodes
questions.explanation: The book says this fault tolerance and resilience "make streaming platforms a good choice when you need a system that can reliably produce, store, and ingest event data."

questions.question: What two categories of upstream stakeholders does the book say a data engineer typically deals with, and what defines each?
options: Systems stakeholders, who build and maintain the source systems (software engineers, application developers, third parties), and data stakeholders, who own and control access to the data (IT, a data governance group, or third parties)
Executives, who approve budgets, and analysts, who write reports
Customers, who use products, and vendors, who sell them
Only a single engineering team with no distinction
questions.explanation: The book defines systems stakeholders as those who build and maintain source systems and data stakeholders as those who "own and control access to the data you want," noting they are often different people and sometimes the same.

questions.question: What does the book call among the most overlooked areas where data engineers can get a lot of value?
options: Creating a feedback loop between data engineers and stakeholders of the source systems to create awareness of how data is consumed and used
Writing perfect SQL for every pipeline
Purchasing the newest orchestration tool
Hiring more data analysts
questions.explanation: The book says creating this feedback loop "is among the single most overlooked areas where data engineers can get a lot of value," so engineers are made aware of upstream impacts such as schema or data changes.

questions.question: Where does the book say data contracts should be stored, and how should they be formatted?
options: In a well-known, easy-to-find location such as a GitHub repo or internal documentation site, and ideally in a standardized form so they can be integrated into development or queried programmatically
In a private personal notebook
Only in email correspondence
As unformatted prose in a wiki nobody reads
questions.explanation: The book recommends storing data contracts "in a well-known and easy-to-find location such as a GitHub repo or internal documentation site" and formatting them in a standardized form.

questions.question: How does the book characterize the data engineer's control over source systems and their undercurrents?
options: Source systems are generally outside the control of the data engineer, and there's an implicit assumption that their stakeholders follow best practices for data management, DataOps, and other undercurrents
Data engineers fully own and operate every source system
Source systems never involve other stakeholders
Undercurrents never apply to source systems
questions.explanation: The book says "source systems are generally outside the control of the data engineer," with an implicit assumption that owners follow best practices; the engineer should get as much upstream support as possible.

questions.question: Which security considerations does the book list for source systems?
options: Whether data is encrypted at rest and in transit, whether you access the source over the public internet or a VPN, keeping credentials locked away (key manager, password manager, or SSO), and trusting but verifying the source system
Only whether the source has a firewall
Only whether the source uses HTTPS
Security of source systems is never the engineer's concern
questions.explanation: The book lists all four areas, concluding "always be sure to trust but verify that the source system is legitimate."

questions.question: What does the book say about data management of source systems from a data engineer's perspective?
options: In most cases you will have only peripheral control, if any, so you should understand how data is managed upstream since it directly influences ingestion, storage, and transformation
Data engineers have total control over upstream data management
Data management of source systems is irrelevant to pipelines
Source systems cannot be governed or documented
questions.explanation: The book says "in most cases, you will have only peripheral control—if any control at all—over source systems and the data they produce," and that understanding upstream management directly influences how you ingest, store, and transform data.

questions.question: Which data-management areas does the book list to consider about source systems, and what privacy question does it raise?
options: Data governance, data quality, schema changes, master data management, privacy and ethics, and regulatory requirements — including whether you have access to raw data or it will be obfuscated, how long it's retained, and whether it shifts locations
Only storage cost and query performance
Only the number of tables in the source
Privacy and regulatory concerns never apply to source systems
questions.explanation: The book lists these areas and raises questions about raw versus obfuscated data, retention, location shifts, and whether regulations even permit access.

questions.question: Why does the book say operational excellence (DevOps, DataOps, MLOps, XOps) should extend up and down the entire stack?
options: So the data engineering lifecycle is supported at both ends, even though it's often not fully realized in practice
So that only the data engineering team can be blamed for failures
Because source system teams never need operational practices
It is required by law
questions.explanation: The book says "operational excellence... should extend up and down the entire stack and support the data engineering and lifecycle. While this is ideal, it's often not fully realized."

questions.question: What DataOps observability checks does the book recommend for source systems?
options: Set up monitoring for source system uptime and checks that data conforms to expectations — e.g. is the data good quality, is the schema conformant, are customer records consistent, and is data hashed as stipulated by internal policy
Only monitor the data warehouse
Only track the number of tables
Observability of source systems is impossible
questions.explanation: The book lists these exact checks under DataOps observability, including schema conformance, record consistency, and policy-stipulated hashing.

questions.question: What incident-response planning does the book recommend for source system failures?
options: Plan how your pipeline behaves if a source system goes offline and how to backfill the "lost" data once the system is back online
Ignore the failure until analysts complain
Delete the affected pipeline entirely
Shift the incident to the source system team with no plan
questions.explanation: The book asks: "How will your data pipeline behave if a source system goes offline? What's your plan to backfill the 'lost' data once the source system is back online?"

questions.question: What four factors does the book list for understanding source system architecture strengths and weaknesses?
options: Reliability, durability, availability, and people
Cost, speed, color, and branding
Schema, index, query, and cache
Only uptime percentage
questions.explanation: The book discusses source system architectures under reliability, durability, availability, and people (who's in charge of the design).

questions.question: What does the book say about reliability and durability of source systems?
options: All systems suffer from entropy — outputs drift, bugs are introduced, and glitches happen; and everything eventually fails, so you must account for how an inevitable failure or outage will affect your managed data systems
Reliable systems never fail and durable systems cannot lose data
Reliability and durability are the same concept
Source systems are guaranteed to be perfectly reliable
questions.explanation: The book says "all systems suffer from entropy at some point" under reliability, and under durability: "everything fails... you need to account for how an inevitable failure or outage will affect your managed data systems."

questions.question: What orchestration considerations does the book raise for accessing source systems?
options: Ensuring your orchestration has correct network access, authentication, and authorization; understanding data availability cadence (fixed schedule vs whenever); and deciding whether to share common frameworks such as Kubernetes or Airflow with the application team while balancing integration benefits against tight-coupling risk
Only the brand of orchestration tool
Only the number of DAGs
Orchestration never touches source systems
questions.explanation: The book says orchestration mainly requires "the correct network access, authentication, and authorization," plus cadence/frequency and common-framework decisions with no single correct answer.

questions.question: What software-engineering considerations does the book list for writing code to access a source system?
options: Networking (HTTPS, SSH, VPN), authentication and authorization (credentials stored safely, correct IAM roles), access patterns (API pagination, driver compatibility, retries and timeouts), orchestration integration, parallelization, and deployment
Only variable naming conventions
Only code formatting style
Software engineering skills are not needed for source access
questions.explanation: The book lists exactly these six areas: networking, authentication/authorization, access patterns, orchestration, parallelization, and deployment.

questions.question: What does the book warn about data engineers who treat source systems as "someone else's problem"?
options: They do so at their peril — data engineers who abuse source systems may need to look for another job when production goes down
It is the recommended best practice
Source systems never affect production
There are no consequences for ignoring source systems
questions.explanation: The book says "data engineers tend to treat source systems as 'someone else's problem'—do this at your peril! Data engineers who abuse source systems may need to look for another job when production goes down."

questions.question: What benefits does the book say better collaboration with source system teams can bring?
options: Higher-quality data, more successful outcomes, and better data products
Lower salaries for data engineers
Elimination of all pipelines
Guaranteed zero incidents
questions.explanation: The book says "if there's a stick, there's also a carrot. Better collaboration with source system teams can lead to higher-quality data, more successful outcomes, and better data products."

questions.question: How does the book describe the growing integration between data engineers and source system teams?
options: Reverse ETL has risen into prominence, an event-streaming platform can serve event-driven architectures and analytics, and a source system can also be a data engineering system — so build shared systems where it makes sense
The two teams should never interact
Source systems can never be data engineering systems
Reverse ETL has been deprecated permanently
questions.explanation: The book notes reverse ETL's rise, that a source system can also be a data engineering system, and advises to "build shared systems where it makes sense to do so."

questions.question: What does the book recommend for building user-facing value with application teams?
options: Look for opportunities to build user-facing data products, talk to application teams about analytics they'd like to present to users or places where ML could improve the user experience, and make application teams stakeholders in data engineering
Keep all data products internal
Avoid discussing ML with application teams
Wait for application teams to come to you
questions.explanation: The book gives exactly this advice in its conclusion, including making application teams stakeholders and sharing successes.
